name: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE)

lead: SARPE widens the upper jaw in adults whose palate suture has fused, giving a broader upper arch, roomier bite and, as forum posters hope, a fuller, better-proportioned midface and smile.

A surgeon makes bone cuts to release the maxilla, then an expander is turned gradually while new bone fills the gap. It is a recognized treatment for transverse maxillary deficiency, a narrow upper jaw that can cause crossbite and crowding. Clinical literature reports dental and skeletal outcomes rather than facial appearance.

paras: It is planned with an orthodontist, done under general anaesthesia, and the expander is turned daily for a few weeks, followed by months of retention and usually braces. Alternatives such as miniscrew-assisted expansion (MARPE) have been developed for some adults.
Reviews catalogue complications. Common effects include discomfort, swelling and a gap between the front teeth. The procedure involves general anaesthesia and bone cuts, with recovery restrictions.

angle.text: Adults who want a wider upper jaw use SARPE when non-surgical expansion is no longer an option, and forum posters link the widening to a fuller, better-proportioned face. Skeletal widening is established for narrow-jaw bite problems; its facial-appearance effects are mostly reported anecdotally.

lead: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE), also called SARME (surgically assisted rapid maxillary expansion), is a combined surgical and orthodontic procedure that widens the upper jaw in people whose midpalatal suture has fused after puberty. An oral and maxillofacial surgeon makes bone cuts that release the resistance around the maxilla, and an expander appliance fitted by the orthodontist is then turned gradually so that new bone fills the gap.[1][2][3][4]

For appearance, the appeal people describe is a broader upper jaw: a wider smile arch with fewer 'narrow' dental corridors, more room for the teeth, and, in looksmaxxing discussion, a wider midface because the maxilla is treated as the keystone that other facial bones hang from.[5] Clinically the procedure is established as a treatment for transverse maxillary deficiency, a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower that can cause posterior crossbite and crowding, and it is also described in connection with nasal airway width and some cases of obstructive sleep apnea.[6][2][4][1]

Research on SARPE is substantial and mostly orthodontic: case series from the early 1990s, randomized trials of retention and surgical technique, and systematic reviews of expansion amounts, relapse, asymmetry and complications.[7][8][9][10][11] Studies measure dental and skeletal width, bite correction and, in some, nasal airflow; they generally do not rate facial attractiveness, which is the point where clinical literature and forum discussion differ.[12][10]

Non-surgical alternatives, chiefly miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE), have been developed to avoid surgery in some young adults, and the choice between the two is an active topic in the literature.[13][14][12][15]

paras: In growing children and adolescents, tooth-borne expanders can separate the midpalatal suture, but expansion in adults is slower and more uncomfortable and tends to become mostly dental rather than skeletal.[2][3] SARPE adds osteotomies (surgical bone cuts) to release the bony resistances around the maxilla before the expander is activated.[1][2] The Wikipedia article on the procedure lists its indications as skeletal maturity with a fused suture, a narrow upper jaw (transverse maxillary hypoplasia), bilateral posterior crossbite, failure of other expansion devices, crowding from insufficient arch space, and obstructive sleep apnea in people with a narrow palate.[4]

The surgical technique varies. The Wikipedia description has the surgeon making Le Fort I-style cuts without fully down-fracturing the maxilla, with an optional separation of the pterygoid plates (pterygomaxillary disjunction, PMD), which some surgeons omit because of the risk of injuring the pterygoid venous plexus.[4] A 2016 systematic review of three studies (48 patients, 25 with and 23 without PMD) used tooth-borne hyrax-type expanders, a latency period of 3 to 7 days, and activation of roughly half a millimetre a day, and found the evidence on PMD inconclusive.[8][4]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, describes a typical sequence: a tooth-borne expander placed before surgery, a latency of several days, gradual activation, and retention of the device for four to six months while bone forms, followed by braces.[1] The same page describes operating time of under an hour and recovery guidance such as a liquid then soft diet for several weeks and avoiding contact sports.[1] SARPE addresses the side-to-side dimension; the Wikipedia article notes it is sometimes followed by a Le Fort I osteotomy to correct vertical and front-to-back problems.[4]

Palatal expansion itself dates to the 19th century. Wikipedia credits Emerson Angell with the first paper in 1860, describing a screw placed between the premolars of a teenager; the idea met opposition from some contemporaries, and Andrew Haas reintroduced rapid expansion in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s.[3] The tooth-borne Hyrax expander was introduced by Biederman in 1968, and bonded expanders followed in 1973.[3]

Surgical assistance came later. Wikipedia lists a surgical technique described by Brown in 1938, corticotomies discussed by Kole in 1959 and a midline split with grafting described by Steinhauser in 1972.[4] Grokipedia adds osteotomies described in 1969, conservative adult series in the 1980s and a less traumatic osteotomy approach in the 1990s, though the page itself carries accuracy caveats.[1] An outpatient SARPE technique with long-term stability, reported in 19 patients with a mean age of 30, appeared in 1992.[7] A 1997 report addressed management of transverse maxillary deficiency with SARPE, and bone-borne transpalatal distraction, intended to avoid anchorage loss and root resorption seen with tooth-borne devices, was described in 1999 and 2001.[16][17][18]
From about 2010, miniscrew-anchored devices created a non-surgical route for some young adults.[13][14] Reviews published in the 2020s compare the side effects of the two approaches.[12]

A literature review in 2008 summarized SARPE as having gradually gained popularity for correcting transverse deficiency in skeletally mature patients, where correction is harder than in young patients.[6] A European Journal of Orthodontics study examined the skeletal and dental changes that follow it.[2] In the 1992 outpatient series, relapse averaged 8.8 percent in the canine region, 1 percent at the premolars and 7.7 percent at the molars after about 2.4 years.[7] Grokipedia reports roughly 3.5 mm of skeletal expansion out of about 7.5 mm total at the first molars, the remainder being dental tipping, and relapse of roughly 5 to 25 percent.[1]

Stability has been tested in trials. A randomized trial of 30 adults compared a transpalatal arch retainer with no retention after the expander remained in place for four months.[11] A controlled trial followed SARPE and orthopedic expansion for three years.[19] Per the Wikipedia article, Chamberland and Proffit reported that skeletal expansion of roughly 3 to 4 mm was stable, that about a third of dental expansion was lost, and that stability was similar to other expansion methods.[4]

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven studies found that after SARPE the SNA angle increased by about 0.5 degrees and the SN-PP angle by about 0.6 degrees, small changes in the maxilla's forward and vertical position.[10] A 2022 systematic review of 13 articles put the prevalence of uneven left-right expansion at 7.52 percent.[9]

On the face and airway, Wikipedia and Grokipedia note benefits for nasal airflow, and Grokipedia cites nasal cavity volume increases of about 21 to 23 percent in several studies.[4][1] A rhinomanometry study examined respiratory function after orthodontic-surgical treatment, and trials of expansion methods on nasomaxillary structures and of MARPE in sleep apnea have been registered.[20][21][22] The clinical literature measures dental, skeletal and airway outcomes; no study located rates facial attractiveness after SARPE.

A 2002 review and case report catalogued complications of SARPE.[23] A 2025 scoping review screened 746 articles, included 26 (11 retrospective, 12 prospective, 3 randomized) and grouped the side effects reported for SARPE and MARPE in adults into categories to inform treatment choice.[12] Grokipedia lists temporary pain and swelling, nosebleeds, palatal ulceration, gum recession, temporary numbness in the cheek and a gap between the upper front teeth, and notes that its own complication figures conflict across sections.[1] Wikipedia lists an unaesthetic period during expansion, the need for a post-operative expander, dependence on patient compliance, a likely second surgery and pterygoid plexus risk.[4]

General effects described for palatal expanders include speech difficulty and extra saliva, headaches and pain on turning, tongue sores, a diastema that may later be closed with braces, and thinning of the buccal bone.[3] Bone-borne distraction was developed partly to address anchorage loss, relapse, cortical fenestration and buccal root resorption seen with tooth-borne devices.[17] The procedure uses general anesthesia in standard cases and is performed by oral and maxillofacial surgeons.[1][4]

MARPE anchors the expander to the palate with two to four mini-implants and, according to Wikipedia, is less invasive than SARPE and produces more skeletal than dental change, though most adults, especially men, may still need a surgical assist for consistent results.[3] A miniscrew-assisted method was devised in 2010 so that some patients could avoid a two-stage surgical approach and its periodontal effects and relapse.[13] A later report described non-surgical treatment of transverse deficiency in adults with microimplant-assisted expansion.[14] A 2021 article compared microimplant-assisted and surgically assisted expansion for maxillary transverse discrepancy.[15] Segmental Le Fort I osteotomy is another surgical comparator under trial.[24] Slow expansion, in which the screw is turned about 1 mm a week, is described for growing patients.[3]

SARPE is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as an adult alternative to mewing and to expansion approaches meant for adolescents. A thread presents it as simpler and better designed for people past puberty and argues that the maxilla acts as a hinge for the other facial bones.[5] The thread's author states that non-surgical expansion has minimal effect after about 16 and none after 25.[5] A reply quotes a cost for orthognathic surgery in Spain starting around 15,000 euros and up to 40,000 euros in complex cases, noting that it is often treated as cosmetic and not insured.[5]

Patients also describe SARPE outside appearance contexts: a poster on a T Nation sleep-apnea thread reported having maxillary surgical expansion after a cephalometric assessment found a narrow upper jaw, with a persistent diastema afterwards.[25] Such accounts appear alongside clinical interest in expansion for airway reasons.[4][22]

Clinical research includes reviews and cohort studies of skeletal and dental changes and complications.[6][2][23] Systematic reviews address pterygomaxillary disjunction, asymmetric expansion and sagittal-vertical maxillary change.[8][9][10] Randomized trials cover retention and stability and the use of piezosurgery versus saw and burrs for patient morbidity.[11][19] Registered randomized trials include a three-segment versus two-segment technique trial (50 patients), a comparison of two SARME techniques (20 patients), a trial comparing segmental Le Fort I with SARME (90 patients), a study of expansion methods on nasomaxillary structures (30 patients, recruiting) and tooth-borne versus hybrid expanders (32 patients, not yet recruiting).[26][27][24][21][28]

lore.intro: SARPE is discussed on looksmax.org as an adult route to a wider maxilla when other expansion options are considered unavailable; discussion overlaps with threads on mewing, MARPE and orthognathic surgery.[5]

claims.claim: SARPE widens the maxilla in adults, which also widens and improves the face.
Non-surgical methods such as mewing or MSE stop working after adolescence or about age 25.
The procedure is expensive and is classed as cosmetic.
SARPE is more stable than other ways of widening the jaw.

Brown described as having reported a surgical SARPE technique.[4]
